cases.rationale: Qxb6 meets the a7 threat by taking its source. Bxa3 instead admits the underpromotion on b8, while the queenside pawn tension survives after other choices.

Bxe6 and Rxf2 change the bishop and rook exchanges. The advanced pawn on e6 and resulting central pawn control shape the quieter continuation.
The knight capture or check changes Black's ability to take d6 and trade on b8. White's a-pawn and the rook blockade remain different strategic concerns.
gxf1=R+ or gxf1=Q+ gives a concrete capture and reply. The black g-pawn continues to restrict White's king and knight across the choices.
Taking immediately on c6 prevents c7. After Nd5 or Qa7, stopping the same pawn takes a different rook and bishop exchange on c7.
Qxd6 allows the queen sacrifice and knight fork. Other moves keep different control of the d-file and can permit the promotion after the rook exchanges.

The a-pawn advances and trades for White's rook in the leading lines. White's rook remains tied to a1 and other pieces must be placed with that restriction in mind.
Ra2 restrains the pawn from behind, even after the checking move ...f5+. The bishop move allows immediate promotion and the rook can seek checks instead.
Exchanges on b8 and f7 allow the black b-pawn to advance. White's rook and queen placement change whether it can promote in the sampled lines.
Nf4 changes the consequence of Qxe3 through Nxh3+. The other preparations shift the support of the advanced e3 pawn and the central file.
The queen checks route toward d3 and the rook invasion on c1 provide a forcing threat. The sampled lines leave the distinct contribution of the c6 pawn unclear.

The initial b-pawn trade and White's rook placement determine how Black can play against the advanced d-pawn and a-file pawn tension.
